cards.explanation: The answer is blind. Verse 10 says, “Israel’s watchmen are blind, they are all oblivious…” (Isaiah 56:10). A watchman is there to spot trouble early, and these ones aren't seeing any of it. That's why the verse is so serious, friends.
The answer is False. Verse 10 calls them mute dogs that cannot bark. A dog that can't bark at the burglar is basically a very furry doorstop. The picture is of watchmen who aren't warning anybody.

The answer is discernment, bakers. Verse 11 calls them shepherds with no discernment, and says they all turn to their own way. Those two go together in the verse. It's like a baker who can't tell when the cookies are done and just walks off.
The answer is his own gain, friends. Verse 11 says each one is seeking his own gain. That's a baker who takes the whole cookie box home and tells the guests the oven broke.

The answer is like today only far better. They say, “…tomorrow will be like today, only far better!” (Isaiah 56:12). It's somebody sitting down with a tray of cookies, saying tomorrow will be just like today, only bigger. They're planning on more of the same, with extra.

The answer is that they are taken from the presence of evil. Verse 1 says no one considers that the righteous are taken away from the presence of evil. I think this one is tender, friends. Verse 2 follows with those who walk uprightly entering into peace.

The answer is True. Verse 2 says those who walk uprightly enter into peace, and “they find rest, lying down in death.” It's a quiet verse, and I think a comforting one. Notice the word peace shows up here, and it comes back at the end of the passage.

The answer is True. God asks, “Are you not children of transgression, offspring of deceit…” (Isaiah 57:4). It's a hard question. God asks it right after asking whom they're mocking and sneering at. This is one of the heavier parts of the passage.

The answer is whether He should relent because of them. God asks, “Should I relent because of these?” (Isaiah 57:6). He asks it about the drink offering and the grain offering given to the smooth stones. He's asking, not telling, and the question hangs there.
The answer is forsaking. Verse 8 says, “Forsaking Me…” and then goes on to the uncovered bed. It's God Himself saying it. The bed on the hill and the memorial behind the door come with leaving Him.

The answer is a great distance, friends. Verse 9 says they sent their envoys, the messengers they sent out, a great distance. That's the long-haul route, not a quick errand. Those envoys earned every mile.
The answer is False. God says in verse 10 that they did not say, “There is no hope!” They found renewal of their strength, so they didn't grow weak. Tired, yes, but still on the road.

The answer is that He has long been silent. God asks, “Is it not because I have long been silent that you do not fear Me?” (Isaiah 57:11). It's a question He puts to them, and the verse leaves it as a question, friends.

The answer is False. In verse 12 God says, “I will expose your righteousness and your works, and they will not profit you.” So all that effort doesn't pay them back. It's like stamping a hundred cookies and not one of them going in the box.

The answer is idols, bakers. God says, “…let your companies of idols deliver you!” (Isaiah 57:13). A crowd of idols, and not one of them is a rescuer. The crowd looks impressive, and that's about all it has going for it.
The answer is True. God says, “…the wind will carry off all of them, a breath will take them away.” (Isaiah 57:13). It's like a receipt blowing across a parking lot. Gone with one gust.

The answer is whoever seeks refuge in God. God says, “…he who seeks refuge in Me will inherit the land and possess My holy mountain.” (Isaiah 57:13). The one who seeks refuge in God gets the inheritance. That's a nice turn after all those idols.

The answer is the oppressed and humble in spirit. The Holy One says, “I dwell in a high and holy place, and with the oppressed and humble in spirit…” (Isaiah 57:15). He's high and holy, and He's also near the humble. I love that both are in the same verse.

The answer is True. Verse 15 says He is there to “…revive the heart of the contrite.” The contrite are the ones who are humble and sorry. A revived heart is a good thing to have after a long stretch of rough days.

The answer is that man's spirit would grow weak before Him, friends. God says, “for then the spirit of man would grow weak before Me—the breath of life I have made.” (Isaiah 57:16). He ties it to the breath of life He made. It's His own reason, and He gives it.

The answer is True. Verse 17 says, “yet he kept turning back to the desires of his heart.” God struck him, and he still kept turning back. This is a heavy verse. It makes what comes next in verse 18 stand out all the more.

The answer is heal, friends. God says, “I have seen his ways, but I will heal him…” (Isaiah 57:18). He's seen it all, and the word that follows the ‘but’ is heal. That ‘but’ is the best word in the verse.
The answer is False. In verse 19 the LORD says, “Peace, peace to those far and near…” and says He will heal them. He says peace twice, and He says it to the far ones too.

The answer is be still. Verse 20 says the wicked are like the storm-tossed sea, because “…it cannot be still…” It's a washing machine stuck on spin with a lopsided load. The waves keep going and going.

The answer is False. Verse 21 closes the passage by saying there is no peace for the wicked. It comes right after the picture of the storm-tossed sea that cannot be still. It's a sober ending, so I'll let it sit.
